summary: Describes ISATAP, which connects dual-stack IPv6/IPv4 nodes across an IPv4 network by treating the IPv4 network as a link layer for IPv6. It provides automatic tunneling similar to a non-broadcast multiple access model. It replaces RFC 4214. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: ISATAP lets dual-stack computers communicate with IPv6 across an IPv4 network inside a site. It builds an IPv6 interface identifier from an IPv4 address and uses that address to carry IPv6 packets in IPv4.

subtitle: Automatic IPv6 tunneling between dual-stack nodes across an IPv4 network within a site.

tldr.problem: Dual-stack nodes in a site may need IPv6 communication even when the network between them carries IPv4.
tldr.mechanism: ISATAP treats the IPv4 network as an IPv6 link, embeds a node's IPv4 address in an IPv6 interface identifier, and tunnels IPv6 packets over IPv4.
tldr.outcome: The Informational memo replaces RFC 4214 and describes use within sites that follow its security considerations. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 5214 is an Informational document published in March 2008. It obsoletes RFC 4214; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 5214.

sections.title: What ISATAP Does
sections.content:
The Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP) connects dual-stack IPv6/IPv4 nodes over IPv4 networks. It treats the IPv4 network as a link layer for IPv6 and automatically tunnels IPv6 packets inside IPv4.

The memo applies to ISATAP nodes within sites that meet its security considerations, including certain enterprise and wireless-operator networks. It covers host-to-router, router-to-host, and host-to-host tunneling; extensions beyond this scope are not addressed.
sections.plainLanguage: ISATAP carries IPv6 packets across a site's IPv4 network. Both ends need to support IPv6 and IPv4, and the network must meet the memo's security conditions.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Locators
sections.content:
An ISATAP interface identifier uses Modified EUI-64 format. It combines the 24-bit IANA OUI 00-00-5E, the 8-bit value 0xFE, and a 32-bit IPv4 address in network byte order. The universal/local bit is set to 1 when the IPv4 address is known to be globally unique and to 0 otherwise.

An ISATAP interface maintains a locator set of IPv4 address-to-interface mappings from one site; a locator set MUST NOT span multiple sites. The interface uses IPv4 addresses in this set to create link-local ISATAP addresses. Since wide-area IPv4 multicast cannot be assumed, the memo assumes the IPv4 carrier network provides unicast, and does not specify IPv6 multicast over ISATAP.
sections.plainLanguage: The interface identifier contains a site's IPv4 address in a defined position. A router uses the address in that identifier to determine where to send the IPv6 packet inside IPv4.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Packet Checks
sections.content:
ISATAP maps an IPv6 address to a link-layer address by treating the last four octets as an IPv4 address. This allows a node to encapsulate an IPv6 packet in an IPv4 datagram without a separate address lookup.

When a node receives an IPv4 protocol 41 datagram that does not belong to a configured tunnel, it checks whether the IPv4 destination and arrival interface match a locator in an ISATAP interface's locator set. If a match exists, it MUST check that the IPv4 source is consistent with the encapsulated IPv6 source: either the IPv6 address embeds that IPv4 address, or the IPv4 source belongs to the Potential Router List.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks the outer IPv4 address against the address embedded in the inner IPv6 packet, or checks that the sender is a listed router. This helps reject packets with mismatched source information.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery and Router Lists
sections.content:
ISATAP uses IPv6 Neighbor Discovery with additions for the Potential Router List (PRL). The PRL contains IPv4 addresses for routers that advertise ISATAP service, each associated with a timer. A node can initialize it through manual configuration, a DNS name, a DHCPv4 vendor-specific option, or another method.

The default PRL refresh interval is 3600 seconds. A host sends Router Solicitations directly to PRL entries, and routers send Solicited Router Advertisements directly to the requesting host. A received advertisement is accepted only when its link-local ISATAP source embeds the IPv4 address of a PRL entry. Timer values must observe the configured minimum solicitation interval; an example conservative default is 2 minutes. ISATAP hosts SHOULD perform Neighbor Unreachability Detection; routers MAY do so.
sections.plainLanguage: A node keeps a list of possible ISATAP routers and asks them directly for network information. It checks that an advertisement came from a router on that list.

sections.title: Site Administration and Security
sections.content:
Site administrators maintain the PRL, commonly through a fully qualified domain name in the site's name service. The memo encourages the name convention isatap.domainname and recommends conservative DNS TTL values to limit control traffic.

The memo identifies spoofed IPv4 protocol 41 packets from outside or inside a site as threats. Border routers should apply IPv4 ingress filtering and protocol 41 filtering to limit outside injection. Administrators should keep the PRL current and protect its resolution mechanism from subversion. IPv4 protection does not protect IPv6 traffic after it leaves the ISATAP domain, so IPv6 security is still required.
sections.plainLanguage: Administrators must control which routers appear in the PRL and filter unauthorized protocol 41 traffic. Protecting the IPv4 tunnel alone does not secure IPv6 traffic beyond the site.
